queue.tree_name: The Weeping Cedar of the Vallée-aux-Loups (Cèdre pleureur)
queue.tree_species: Blue Weeping Atlas Cedar (Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca Pendula')
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the props: about thirty resin supports shaped like stalagmites, holding up branches that sweep the ground across an area the size of a tennis court. It is the tree you can walk in underneath.
queue.story:
Every blue weeping Atlas cedar in the world came off this one tree. The cultivar Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca Pendula' appeared here as a mutation around 1873, and every specimen since has been a cutting or a graft descended from it. If you have seen one draped over a lawn in a park or a garden somewhere, you have seen a copy of this.

It is about 150 years old, roughly five metres round and only 14 metres tall, and it spreads its branches across about 700 square metres, near enough a tennis court. The department calls it the largest of its kind anywhere, which more or less follows from being the first.
